description: Dynamic programming decomposed. The methodology: recognise overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure, define a recurrence, evaluate it efficiently. Memoisation (top-down recursion + cache) vs tabulation (bottom-up loop). Space optimisation via rolling arrays. Classic problems: LCS, edit distance, knapsack, matrix chain, coin change.

sub_mechanisms.name: optimal_substructure
sub_mechanisms.definition: Property: the optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems. Shortest path has it (subpath is shortest); longest simple path doesn't (can't reuse vertices).
sub_mechanisms.why: Necessary for DP to work. Without it, combining subproblem solutions doesn't give the optimal whole. Recognising this property is the first DP design step.

sub_mechanisms.name: overlapping_subproblems
sub_mechanisms.definition: Property: naive recursion computes the same subproblem many times. Fibonacci recursion computes Fib(k) exponentially many times.
sub_mechanisms.why: If subproblems didn't overlap, divide-and-conquer would suffice. Overlap is what makes memoisation a huge speedup. The exponential-to-polynomial transformation comes from caching repeated work.

sub_mechanisms.name: memoisation_top_down
sub_mechanisms.definition: Recursive function with cache. On each call: if argument seen before, return cached. Otherwise compute, cache, return.
sub_mechanisms.why: Easy to add to existing recursive code. Python's @functools.cache decorator. Only computes subproblems actually needed. Recursion overhead + cache lookup per call.

sub_mechanisms.name: tabulation_bottom_up
sub_mechanisms.definition: Iterative filling of DP table from base cases up to the target. Loop structure encodes evaluation order.
sub_mechanisms.why: Better cache locality (sequential array access). No recursion overhead. Compiler-friendly. Often 2-3x faster than memoised version with the same algorithm.

sub_mechanisms.name: DP_state_definition
sub_mechanisms.definition: What does dp[i][j] mean? Defining the state precisely is the hard part of DP. Common patterns: dp[i] = best answer using first i items; dp[i][j] = best answer for ranges, intervals, configurations.
sub_mechanisms.why: Wrong state → can't write a correct recurrence. Right state makes the recurrence obvious. The state's dimensionality affects time + space complexity. Hardest part of DP design.

sub_mechanisms.name: DP_recurrence
sub_mechanisms.definition: Equation defining dp[state] in terms of dp[smaller states]. E.g., LCS: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if a[i] == b[j], else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
sub_mechanisms.why: The algorithm IS the recurrence. Correctness reduces to verifying the recurrence. Once correct, implementation is mechanical (memoise or tabulate).

sub_mechanisms.name: DP_base_cases
sub_mechanisms.definition: Trivial cases handled directly: dp[0] = 0 (Fibonacci); dp[i][0] = i (edit distance from i chars to empty).
sub_mechanisms.why: Recurrence needs a ground to stand on. Wrong base case → wrong answer despite correct recurrence. Often subtle for off-by-one or boundary semantics.

sub_mechanisms.name: rolling_array_space_optimisation
sub_mechanisms.definition: When DP only depends on previous row: store just two rows (current + previous). Or one row updated carefully.
sub_mechanisms.why: Reduces space from O(n²) to O(n) when applicable. LCS, edit distance, knapsack all admit this optimisation. Critical for problems too large to fit a 2D table in memory.

sub_mechanisms.name: reconstruction_from_DP_table
sub_mechanisms.definition: After filling table, trace back from the answer to recover the actual solution (not just the optimal value).
sub_mechanisms.why: DP value gives 'minimum cost'; reconstruction gives 'which operations'. Often O(n + m) backward walk through the table. Used in diff, sequence alignment, optimal path recovery.

sub_mechanisms.name: knapsack_01_DP
sub_mechanisms.definition: dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w. Recurrence: max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - weight[i]] + value[i]).
sub_mechanisms.why: Classical 0/1 knapsack. O(n·W) where W is capacity. Pseudo-polynomial: linear in W but W can be exponential in input size (bits). This is the difference between weakly and strongly NP-hard.

sub_mechanisms.name: interval_DP
sub_mechanisms.definition: State = interval [i, j]. Recurrence considers all split points k between i and j. Matrix chain multiplication, optimal BST, palindrome partitioning.
sub_mechanisms.why: Common DP pattern when problem structure decomposes naturally into intervals. O(n³) typical: n² states × n split points.

sub_mechanisms.name: bitmask_DP
sub_mechanisms.definition: State includes a bitmask representing a subset. dp[mask] = best for that subset. Used for TSP and other NP-hard problems with small N.
sub_mechanisms.why: Exponential state space (2^n masks) but polynomial per-state work. Tractable for n ≤ ~20. TSP: O(2^n · n²). Better than O(n!) brute force but still exponential.

derivation_rules.name: DP_correct_iff_optimal_substructure
derivation_rules.why: DP combines optimal subproblem solutions. If the problem doesn't have optimal substructure (longest simple path), the combined result isn't optimal — DP gives wrong answer. Recognising substructure is the gating decision.

derivation_rules.name: memoisation_exponential_to_polynomial
derivation_rules.why: Each distinct subproblem solved once instead of exponentially many times. Naive Fibonacci: O(2^n). Memoised: O(n). The speedup factor equals the redundancy of the original recursion.

derivation_rules.name: tabulation_better_cache_than_memoisation
if: DP table is filled bottom-up in sequential order
derivation_rules.why: Sequential array fill prefetches well. Memoised recursion has unpredictable access pattern + function-call overhead. Same algorithm, 2-3x speedup from tabulation alone. Always tabulate when feasible.

derivation_rules.name: rolling_array_when_only_last_row_matters
if: DP recurrence only references the previous row
then: O(n) space instead of O(n²) is achievable
derivation_rules.why: Just keep two rows (or one with careful update order). LCS, edit distance, knapsack all admit this. Critical for memory-constrained execution. The recurrence structure determines which space optimisations are possible.

derivation_rules.name: pseudo_polynomial_distinguishes_weak_strong_NP
if: DP runtime is polynomial in numeric values but exponential in input size in bits
then: the problem is weakly (not strongly) NP-hard
derivation_rules.why: Knapsack: O(n·W). W can have arbitrary bit-length, so runtime can be exponential in input. Strongly NP-hard problems remain hard even when numeric values are bounded. The distinction informs which pseudo-polynomial algorithms are practical.
